newsitem.title: CHINA: China still far from forming oil reserve - industry.
newsitem.headline: China still far from forming oil reserve - industry.

text.p: China is still a long way from setting up a strategic oil reserve to offset fluctuations on the world oil market, industry officials said on Wednesday.
They said the reserve was needed because of China's growing demand for imported oil but plans were only in their early stages.
"This is something we believe we have to do," an official at China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec) told Reuters.
"But we have several major problems that would have to be resolved first," said the official who asked not to be identified.
The official said that China had not determined where the reserves would be stored and who would finance purchases or cover storage and other costs.
The Business Weekly, published by the China Daily, said on Sunday that China was setting up a nation-wide reserve and that it needed to construct several ports capable of handling large oil tankers.
It quoted Zhu Yu, president of China Petrochemical Consulting Corp, Sinopec's think tank, as saying the reserve was needed to offset world price fluctuations.
China's domestic oil production is rising but not as fast as demand.
Some Chinese oil industry officials estimate imports will reach 50 million tonnes in the year 2000 compared with an estimated 33 million this year.
Chinese officials attending an oil conference in Beijing said that Middle East countries were likely to fill much of the gap between China's domestic supply and demand.
Political instability in the Middle East, however, meant that China would have to ensure it had adequate supplies of crude oil in the event of a crisis that shut off some of its supplies.

"In theory this is a sound idea," said another oil industry official, speaking of the creation of a reserve. "But there are so many details that have to be worked out that for the time being I would expect nothing more than discussions."
The Business Weekly also said China was looking at the prospect of establishing its own ocean-going fleets to carry the additional crude imports.
But industry officials said cost factors would stir considerable debate before any decision was reached.
